fixes.explanation: David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), and that's a big résumé. Still, the prophet never names him in these questions. They point to God alone. Honestly, I'd need a much bigger basket and a lot of help just to try.

You got it, baker. The text says he seeks a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not topple. So he's out looking for an expert to keep his idol standing. That's a lot of effort for something that needs help standing.

Close, but the text says it plainly. He seeks a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not topple. So the man doesn't stop at choosing the wood. He also goes looking for an expert to keep the thing standing.
That's right, baker. The prophet says He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth. That's a seat above the whole circle, not down in it. Quite the view, if you ask me.
A golden temple sounds grand, friend. But the prophet doesn't place God in a temple here. He says He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth. That's a seat above the whole earth.

You got it, baker. The prophet says God sits enthroned above the circle of the earth, and its dwellers are like grasshoppers. That's a small, hopping comparison. Nobody down here is looking down on anybody.

You got it, baker. He leads forth the starry host by number and calls each one by name. Every star is counted and every star has a name. I named six cookie cutter kids and six toppings, and that was plenty of work.

The text doesn't mention hiding stars at all, friend. It says God leads forth the starry host by number and calls each one by name. Hiding I can picture, since I spent years hidden in a junk drawer. But the prophet gives these stars names, not a hiding place.
You got it, baker. The prophet says that because of God's great power and mighty strength, not one of them is missing. Every star is accounted for. The reason he gives is His power and strength.
Not this time, friend. The prophet says that because of His great power and mighty strength, not one of them is missing. Every star is accounted for. The prophet ties that to His power and strength.

Not quite, friend. The text says the opposite. The prophet says the LORD is the everlasting God and that He will not grow tired or weary. Tired and weary is where even youths end up, the prophet says (Isaiah 40:30).
The mighty are a fair guess, friend. But the verse says the LORD gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak. The mighty aren't who the verse names. The faint and the weak are.

The verse doesn't mention fasting, friend. The prophet says those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength. Waiting is the word he picks, and I know waiting isn't easy. I spent years waiting in a junk drawer, so I speak from experience.
You got it, baker. Those who wait upon the LORD will run and not grow weary. Picture a run with no weariness at the end. That's more than I manage on my best day.
